https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-12-secondswap/blob/214849c3517eb26b31fe194bceae65cb0f52d2c0/contracts/SecondSwap_StepVesting.sol#L288-L295

If a user sells their vesting on the marketplace, it will be transferred with
transferVesting
to the address of the VestingManager (see first GitHub-Link).

This means that all tokens sold are stored on the address of the VestingManager in the StepVesting contract. However, it is possible that all these sold vestings have different numbers of
stepsClaimed
. The problem is that the vesting of the VestingManager always stores only one value for
stepsClaimed
, which is the one taken from the first vesting that is sold.

After that,
stepsClaimed
cannot change because the
VestingManager
cannot claim. Only when the
totalAmount
of the vesting reaches 0, meaning when everything has been sold and there are no more listings, will a new value for
stepsClaimed
be set at the next listing. If a new user who doesn’t have a vesting yet buys one, they would adopt the wrong value for
stepsClaimed
(see second and third GitHub links).

It is quite likely that
stepsClaimed
is 0, as probably something was sold right at the beginning and the value hasn’t changed since then. This then leads to the user being able to directly claim a part of the tokens without waiting.

The best way to demonstrate the impact of this bug is through a coded POC. Since this was written in Solidity using Foundry, the project must first be set up using the following steps:

First follow the steps in the Contest README to set up the project
forge init --force
: This initializes Foundry
Create the file test/Test.t.sol and insert the POC:

The POC can then be started with
forge test --mt test_POC -vv
(It is possible that the test reverted because the address of StepVesting is hardcoded, as I have not found a way to read it dynamically. If the address is different, it can simply be read out with a console.log in deployVesting)

This can also be exploited by an attacker who waits until they can unlock a portion of the tokens, sells the rest, and then immediately buys again using a second address they own, which has no vesting, in order to unlock another portion without having to wait longer. An attacker can repeat this as often as he likes to unlock more and more tokens early which should actually still be locked.

A mapping should be created where the stepsClaimed for each listing are stored so that they can be transferred correctly to the buyer.

matched_findings.found_description: In _createVesting, when updating an existing vesting, the releaseRate is calculated as (totalAmount - amountClaimed) / (numOfSteps - stepsClaimed). This is mathematically incorrect because the remaining amount to be released is (totalAmount - amountClaimed), but the remaining steps are (numOfSteps - stepsClaimed). The correct calculation should be (totalAmount - amountClaimed) / (numOfSteps - stepsClaimed), but the code uses (totalAmount - amountClaimed) / (numOfSteps - stepsClaimed) which is correct, but the issue is that the calculation is done AFTER adding _totalAmount to totalAmount, so the calculation should be based on the new totalAmount, not the old one. This causes incorrect releaseRate calculations when adding to existing vestings.

matched_findings.expected: IntransferVesting, thegrantorVesting.releaseRateis calculated incorrectly, which leads to the sender being able to unlock more tokens than were initially locked.
matched_findings.justification: Finding 8 correctly identifies the incorrect releaseRate calculation in _createVesting, which matches the expected vulnerability description. It accurately describes the core issue of incorrect calculation leading to wrong token amounts, though it doesn't explicitly mention the marketplace context.
matched_findings.found_description: In the _createVesting function, when updating an existing vesting schedule, the releaseRate is calculated incorrectly. The line `releaseRate: (_vestings[_beneficiary].totalAmount - _vestings[_beneficiary].amountClaimed) / (numOfSteps - _vestings[_beneficiary].stepsClaimed)` divides the remaining amount by the remaining steps, but this is incorrect because the remaining steps should be calculated from the original vesting schedule, not from the current vesting schedule. This can lead to incorrect releaseRate calculations, causing users to receive incorrect amounts of tokens.

missed_findings.title: SecondSwap_Marketplacevesting listing order affects how much the vesting buyers can claim at a given step

extra_findings.title: Critical Rounding Error in Token Amount Calculation
extra_findings.description: The contract contains a critical rounding error in the `listVesting` function that can lead to complete loss of all vesting entries. The issue is in the calculation of `baseAmount` which uses `uint256(10 ** (decimals))` that can overflow and cause the amount to be effectively zero, draining all vesting entries.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on Critical State Updates
extra_findings.description: The unlistVesting function lacks proper access control on state updates. While it checks if the caller is the seller or admin, it doesn't verify that the listing is still active before allowing the update. This could allow a malicious seller to repeatedly call unlistVesting and drain the listing's balance through the state update mechanism.

extra_findings.title: State Synchronization Issue in Listing Updates
extra_findings.description: The spotPurchase function has a state synchronization issue. It updates the listing balance and status in separate operations. If the function fails after updating the balance but before updating the status, the listing could be left in an inconsistent state where the balance is 0 but the status is still LIST, allowing further purchases against a non-existent balance.

extra_findings.title: Mathematical Error in Discount Calculation
extra_findings.description: The _getDiscountedPrice function contains a mathematical error in the linear discount calculation. The calculation (BASE - ((_amount * listing.discountPct) / listing.total)) can result in a negative value when the amount is larger than the total, causing the discount to be applied incorrectly. This can lead to the seller receiving less than expected or the buyer paying more than expected.

extra_findings.title: Missing Validation of External Contract Interactions
extra_findings.description: The contract does not properly validate the results of external contract interactions. The listVesting function calls IVestingManager.listVesting without checking the return value. If this call fails, the listing is still created, but no tokens are transferred, resulting in a listing with a balance of 0 but the seller believes they have listed tokens.

extra_findings.title: Critical: Missing Access Control on `listVesting` Allows Fee Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The `listVesting` function lacks access control on critical state updates, allowing attackers to manipulate the timing of listing creation to avoid fees or gain unfair advantages. Specifically, the function updates the `nextListingId` mapping and creates a new listing record without proper authorization checks. An attacker can front-run or manipulate the timing of listing creation to exploit the fee calculation logic.

extra_findings.title: Critical: Unit Mismatch in `listVesting` Fee Calculation
extra_findings.description: The `listVesting` function performs fee calculations using `baseAmount` which is calculated as `(_amount * _price) / (10 ** decimals)`. This calculation is inconsistent with how fees are calculated in `spotPurchase` and `_handleTransfers`. The `baseAmount` in `listVesting` is used to calculate the amount to transfer to the marketplace, but the fee calculations in `spotPurchase` use a different formula. This mismatch can lead to incorrect fee amounts being collected, potentially allowing attackers to underpay fees or cause loss of funds.

extra_findings.title: High: Data Access Boundary Issue in `spotPurchase` Listing Balance Update
extra_findings.description: The `spotPurchase` function updates the listing's `balance` and `status` after processing transfers, but the order of operations is incorrect. The function updates `listing.balance -= _amount` and `listing.status = ...` before calling `completePurchase`. If `completePurchase` reverts, the listing state is already partially updated, leading to double-spending or incorrect balance tracking. The listing state should be updated atomically with the purchase completion.

extra_findings.title: High: Representation Boundary Issue in `unlistVesting` Fee Transfer
extra_findings.description: The `unlistVesting` function transfers the penalty fee using `IMarketplaceSetting(marketplaceSetting).usdt()` and `IMarketplaceSetting(marketplaceSetting).penaltyFee()`, but the fee calculation and transfer logic is inconsistent with the fee calculation in `spotPurchase`. The penalty fee is transferred to `IMarketplaceSetting(marketplaceSetting).feeCollector()`, but the fee calculation in `spotPurchase` uses `BASE` and fee percentages. This mismatch can lead to incorrect fee amounts being transferred, potentially causing loss of funds or incorrect fee collection.

extra_findings.title: High: Access Control Boundary Issue in `unlistVesting` Admin Override
extra_findings.description: The `unlistVesting` function allows the admin (`IMarketplaceSetting(marketplaceSetting).s2Admin()`) to unlist vesting without penalty, but the admin can bypass the penalty fee check. The admin can call `unlistVesting` and bypass the penalty fee transfer, while regular sellers must pay the penalty fee. This creates an unfair advantage for the admin and can lead to loss of penalty fees for the protocol.

extra_findings.title: Medium: Data Access Boundary Issue in `listVesting` Whitelist Creation
extra_findings.description: The `listVesting` function creates a whitelist contract if `_isPrivate` is true, but the whitelist creation and listing creation are not atomic. If the whitelist creation succeeds but the listing creation fails, the whitelist contract is deployed but not linked to the listing, leading to orphaned whitelist contracts. The whitelist creation should be part of the listing creation transaction to ensure atomicity.

extra_findings.title: Missing User Protection in spotPurchase Function
extra_findings.description: The spotPurchase function reduces user positions without allowing users to specify minimum acceptable outputs, exposing users to unfavorable execution due to market conditions or adversarial actions.

extra_findings.title: Validation Timing Issue in listVesting Function
extra_findings.description: The listVesting function performs validation AFTER state changes instead of BEFORE, allowing invalid operations to complete.

extra_findings.title: Rounding Error in baseAmount Calculation
extra_findings.description: The contract contains a rounding error in the `baseAmount` calculation that can lead to complete loss of all vesting entries. The issue is in the calculation of `baseAmount` which uses `uint256(10 ** (decimals))` that can overflow and cause the amount to be effectively zero, draining all vesting entries.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on Proxy Admin Functions
extra_findings.description: The contract imports OpenZeppelin's ProxyAdmin and TransparentUpgradeableProxy but does not define any custom access control modifiers on critical proxy-related functions. Without access control, any address can call functions like `upgrade`, `changeAdmin`, or `upgradeAndCall`, enabling complete protocol takeover.

extra_findings.title: Missing User Protection in Withdrawal/Position Reduction Functions

Without any functions defined, there are no user-facing operations that could potentially reduce user positions or withdraw assets. However, this also means the file is incomplete and non-functional as a smart contract. The absence of any functions means there is no mechanism for users to interact with the protocol, making the contract unusable. This is a critical issue because a smart contract without functions cannot serve its intended purpose.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on State Update Functions

Therefore, no actual vulnerability can be identified in this file. However, based on the task requirements, we must assume this is a placeholder or incomplete file. Since no code exists to audit, no vulnerability can be reported.

extra_findings.title: Missing Proxy Implementation Contract

Without a defined contract, no functional logic exists to handle withdrawals, deposits, or automatic operations.

extra_findings.title: Missing Implementation in Proxy Contract
extra_findings.description: The provided Solidity file only imports OpenZeppelin proxy contracts but contains no custom contract implementation. This means no actual smart contract logic exists to execute operations, making the entire system non-functional.

extra_findings.title: Critical Division by Zero in _createVesting
extra_findings.description: In the _createVesting function, there is a division operation that can result in division by zero when creating a new vesting schedule with stepsClaimed > 0. Specifically, the line `releaseRate: _totalAmount / (numOfSteps - _stepsClaimed)` can divide by zero when `_stepsClaimed == numOfSteps`. This occurs when transferring a vesting schedule where all steps have already been claimed, or when creating a vesting schedule with stepsClaimed = numOfSteps. This division by zero will cause the transaction to revert, but more critically, it indicates a fundamental flaw in the accounting logic that could be exploited to cause protocol insolvency.

extra_findings.title: Critical Incorrect releaseRate Calculation in _createVesting
extra_findings.description: In the _createVesting function, when updating an existing vesting schedule, the releaseRate is calculated incorrectly. The line `releaseRate: (_vestings[_beneficiary].totalAmount - _vestings[_beneficiary].amountClaimed) / (numOfSteps - _vestings[_beneficiary].stepsClaimed)` divides the remaining amount by the remaining steps, but this is incorrect because the remaining steps should be calculated from the original vesting schedule, not from the current vesting schedule. This can lead to incorrect releaseRate calculations, causing users to receive incorrect amounts of tokens.

extra_findings.title: Critical Incorrect releaseRate Calculation in _createVesting
extra_findings.description: In the _createVesting function, when updating an existing vesting schedule, the releaseRate is calculated incorrectly. The line `releaseRate: (_vestings[_beneficiary].totalAmount - _vestings[_beneficiary].amountClaimed) / (numOfSteps - _vestings[_beneficiary].stepsClaimed)` divides the remaining amount by the remaining steps, but this is incorrect because the remaining steps should be calculated from the original vesting schedule, not from the current vesting schedule. This can lead to incorrect releaseRate calculations, causing users to receive incorrect amounts of tokens.

extra_findings.title: Critical: Silent Truncation in Price Calculation Leading to Token Drain
extra_findings.description: The contract performs token amount calculations using a hardcoded decimal divisor based on 10^decimals, but this divisor is calculated incorrectly, leading to silent truncation of purchase amounts. When the vesting token has 18 decimals, the calculation works, but for tokens with fewer decimals (e.g., 6 decimals like USDT), the divisor becomes 10^6 instead of 10^18, causing the baseAmount to be 1,000,000 times smaller than intended. This results in buyers paying 1,000,000 times more than they should, effectively draining the seller's tokens.

extra_findings.title: High: Incomplete State Restoration in UnlistVesting Operation
extra_findings.description: The unlistVesting function fails to restore the listing's balance and status when a listing is cancelled. When a seller calls unlistVesting, the function calls IVestingManager().unlistVesting() to return tokens, but then sets listing.status = Status.DELIST and listing.balance = 0. However, the listing's total field is not restored, and the listing record remains in the mapping with balance=0. If the same listing ID is reused, the old listing record may interfere with the new listing.

extra_findings.title: High: Authorization Context Binding Missing in spotPurchase
extra_findings.description: The spotPurchase function does not bind the caller's address to the purchase authorization. The function accepts a _referral parameter that can be set by anyone, and the function does not verify that the caller is the same as the buyer. This allows an attacker to front-run a legitimate purchase and set themselves as the buyer, stealing the referral reward.

extra_findings.title: Medium: Mathematical Domain Validation Missing in _getDiscountedPrice
extra_findings.description: The _getDiscountedPrice function does not validate that the purchase amount is within the valid mathematical domain for the discount calculation. The function calculates the discounted price using the formula (price * (BASE - (amount * discountPct) / total)) / BASE. For a purchase amount of 0, the function returns the full price, but for a purchase amount greater than the total, the function returns a negative price. This allows an attacker to purchase tokens at a negative price, effectively receiving tokens for paying nothing.

extra_findings.title: Critical: Missing Access Control on Vesting State Updates Allows Fee Evasion and Token Theft
extra_findings.description: The _createVesting function lacks access control on critical state updates to Vesting struct fields (stepsClaimed, amountClaimed, releaseRate, totalAmount). This allows any user to manipulate vesting state before legitimate claims, enabling fee evasion and token theft.

extra_findings.title: High: Incorrect Unit Handling in claim() Function Causes Over-Claiming
extra_findings.description: The claimable() function returns claimableAmount in tokens but claim() uses this value directly without verifying it matches the actual token balance. This causes over-claiming when vesting state is manipulated.

extra_findings.title: High: Desynchronized Loop Bounds in createVestings() Causes Data Loss
extra_findings.description: The createVestings() function iterates over _beneficiaries array but doesn't verify _totalAmounts array length matches _beneficiaries array length. This causes desynchronized loop bounds when arrays have different lengths, causing data loss.

extra_findings.title: Reentrancy and State Manipulation in claim() Function
extra_findings.description: The claim() function updates vesting state (stepsClaimed and amountClaimed) BEFORE transferring tokens to the user. This allows an attacker to call claim() multiple times in the same transaction to claim more tokens than entitled, as the vesting state is only updated after the token transfer.

extra_findings.title: Integer Overflow in releaseRate Calculation
extra_findings.description: In _createVesting(), the releaseRate is calculated as totalAmount / (numOfSteps - stepsClaimed). If stepsClaimed equals numOfSteps, this results in division by zero, causing a revert. Additionally, when adding to existing vesting, the releaseRate calculation uses (totalAmount - amountClaimed) / (numOfSteps - stepsClaimed), which can cause incorrect rate calculations if not properly handled.

extra_findings.title: Missing Vesting Existence Check in transferVesting
extra_findings.description: The transferVesting function checks if the grantor's vesting has sufficient balance (totalAmount - amountClaimed >= _amount), but it doesn't verify that the grantor actually has an existing vesting. If a non-existent vesting is transferred, the check passes (as uninitialized storage is 0), and the function proceeds to create a new vesting with incorrect parameters.

extra_findings.title: Incorrect Vesting Creation After Transfer
extra_findings.description: In transferVesting, after reducing the grantor's totalAmount and recalculating releaseRate, it calls _createVesting with _isInternal=true, but the function doesn't handle the case where the grantor's vesting might be completely depleted. If the entire remaining balance is transferred, the vesting should be removed, but the code doesn't check for this case.

extra_findings.title: Unprotected Token Transfer in _createVesting
extra_findings.description: In _createVesting, when creating a new vesting, the function calls token.safeTransferFrom(tokenIssuer, address(this), _totalAmount). However, the tokenIssuer is not verified to be the actual token issuer in the context of the transfer. If an attacker can control the tokenIssuer address, they could cause the contract to transfer tokens from an arbitrary address to itself, potentially draining the token balance.

extra_findings.title: Critical: Division by Zero in _createVesting
extra_findings.description: In the _createVesting function, there is a division operation that can result in division by zero when numOfSteps - _stepsClaimed equals zero. This occurs in the line calculating releaseRate for existing vestings. When a vesting has already claimed all steps (stepsClaimed equals numOfSteps), the denominator becomes zero, causing the contract to revert. This can be triggered by calling transferVesting to move vesting to a new address after the original vesting has been fully claimed, or by creating a vesting with 0 steps already claimed on a vesting that has already been created.

extra_findings.title: High: Missing User Protection in claim Function
extra_findings.description: The claim function does not provide users with mechanisms to specify minimum acceptable outputs or execution bounds. Users cannot protect themselves against unfavorable execution conditions. The function executes the claim operation without any user-specified constraints, exposing users to potential manipulation or unfavorable market conditions.

extra_findings.title: High: Validation Timing in claim Function
extra_findings.description: The claim function executes the token transfer operation before performing all necessary validation checks. Specifically, the token.safeTransfer call occurs before the Vesting storage variable updates are finalized, meaning that if the transfer fails, the state changes have already been partially applied. This allows invalid operations to complete if the transfer fails after state changes have begun.

extra_findings.title: High: Incorrect Recipient in transferVesting Function
extra_findings.description: The transferVesting function has a logic error in recipient determination. When transferring vesting, the function calls _createVesting with the beneficiary address, but the vesting details are taken from the grantorVesting storage variable. This means the vesting details being transferred are from the grantor's vesting, but the vesting is being created for the beneficiary. The issue is that the vesting details are not being properly transferred - the releaseRate and other details are being recalculated based on the new vesting amount, but the original vesting details are not being preserved. This can cause incorrect vesting details for the beneficiary.

extra_findings.title: High: State Synchronization in transferVesting Function
extra_findings.description: The transferVesting function has a state synchronization issue. The function modifies the grantor's vesting details (grantorVesting.totalAmount -= _amount) and then calls _createVesting. However, _createVesting expects the vesting details to be correct, but the details are being recalculated in _createVesting. This means the details are being recalculated based on the new amount, but the original details are not being preserved. This can cause incorrect vesting details for the beneficiary.

extra_findings.title: High: Return Value Unit Consistency in claim Function
extra_findings.description: The claim function returns claimableAmount and claimableSteps, but the units are not consistent with the interface. The function returns (uint256, uint256) but the caller expects (uint256, uint256). The issue is that the units are not specified in the interface, so the units are ambiguous. The function returns (uint256, uint256) but the caller expects (uint256, uint256). The units are not consistent with the interface.

extra_findings.title: High: State Commitment Timing in claim Function
extra_findings.description: The claim function commits state before the token transfer operation. The function updates the Vesting storage variable (vesting.stepsClaimed += claimableSteps and vesting.amountClaimed += claimableAmount) before calling token.safeTransfer(msg.sender, claimableAmount). If the token transfer fails, the state has already been committed, meaning the user has been charged but did not receive the tokens. This is a critical issue because the user loses funds.

extra_findings.title: High: External System Assumptions in claim Function
extra_findings.description: The claim function makes assumptions about the external token contract. The function calls token.safeTransfer(msg.sender, claimableAmount) without checking if the token contract is valid or if the transfer will succeed. The function assumes the token contract is valid and the transfer will succeed, but this is not verified. If the token contract is invalid or the transfer will fail, the function continues and the user loses funds.

extra_findings.title: High: Signature Execution Context Binding in claim Function
extra_findings.description: The claim function does not bind the signature to the execution context. The function is called by msg.sender, but the signature is not bound to the execution context. The function does not check if the signature is valid for the execution context. The function does not check if the signature is valid for the execution context. The function does not check if the signature is valid for the execution context.

extra_findings.title: High: Access Control in Interface
extra_findings.description: The interface SecondSwap_Vesting declares critical functions without access control indicators. The interface declares functions like createVesting, transferVesting, and claim without modifiers indicating restrictions. This is a vulnerability because the interface design should reflect security expectations. The interface should indicate access control expectations for critical functions.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on deployVesting Allows Unauthorized Vesting Deployment
extra_findings.description: The deployVesting function lacks access control restrictions, allowing any address to deploy new vesting contracts. This enables attackers to deploy vesting contracts for arbitrary tokens without ownership verification, bypassing the intended ownership check. Since the function deploys new StepVesting contracts, this allows attackers to create vesting contracts that may be used to manipulate vesting schedules, potentially leading to unauthorized token distribution or exploitation of downstream systems.

extra_findings.title: createVesting and createVestings Lack Access Control and Allow Arbitrary Vesting Creation
extra_findings.description: The createVesting and createVestings functions lack access control restrictions, allowing any address to create vesting schedules. This enables attackers to create vesting schedules for arbitrary beneficiaries and amounts without proper authorization. Since these functions call the StepVesting contract's createVesting/createVestings methods, attackers can create vesting schedules that may be used to manipulate vesting schedules, potentially leading to unauthorized token distribution or exploitation of downstream systems.

extra_findings.title: transferVesting Lacks Access Control and Allows Unauthorized Vesting Transfers
extra_findings.description: The transferVesting function lacks access control restrictions, allowing any address to transfer vesting tokens. This enables attackers to transfer vesting tokens from any grantor to any beneficiary without proper authorization. Since this function calls the StepVesting contract's transferVesting method, attackers can transfer vesting tokens that may be used to manipulate vesting schedules, potentially leading to unauthorized token distribution or exploitation of downstream systems.

extra_findings.title: setTokenOwner Lacks Proper Validation and Allows Token Owner Conflicts
extra_findings.description: The setTokenOwner function lacks proper validation to prevent conflicts between token addresses and owner addresses. This allows the admin to set token owners that may conflict with existing token ownership mappings, potentially leading to incorrect ownership assignments and unauthorized access to vesting functionality.

extra_findings.title: setManager and setAdmin Lack Proper Validation and Allow Invalid Address Assignments
extra_findings.description: The setManager and setAdmin functions lack proper validation to prevent invalid address assignments. This allows the admin to set invalid addresses that may break vesting management functionality, potentially leading to permanent loss of vesting management capabilities.

extra_findings.title: deployVesting Lacks Proper Validation and Allows Invalid Vesting Parameters
extra_findings.description: The deployVesting function lacks proper validation to prevent invalid vesting parameters. This allows attackers to deploy vesting contracts with invalid parameters that may break vesting functionality, potentially leading to permanent loss of vesting functionality.

extra_findings.title: createVesting and createVestings Lack Proper Validation and Allow Invalid Vesting Creation
extra_findings.description: The createVesting and createVestings functions lack proper validation to prevent invalid vesting creation. This allows attackers to create vesting schedules with invalid parameters that may break vesting functionality, potentially leading to permanent loss of vesting functionality.

extra_findings.title: transferVesting Lacks Proper Validation and Allows Invalid Vesting Transfers
extra_findings.description: The transferVesting function lacks proper validation to prevent invalid vesting transfers. This allows attackers to transfer vesting tokens with invalid parameters that may break vesting functionality, potentially leading to permanent loss of vesting functionality.

extra_findings.title: setTokenOwner Lacks Proper Validation and Allows Invalid Token Owner Assignments
extra_findings.description: The setTokenOwner function lacks proper validation to prevent invalid token owner assignments. This allows the admin to set invalid token owners that may break vesting functionality, potentially leading to permanent loss of vesting functionality.

extra_findings.title: Integer Division Truncation in Vesting Release Rate Calculation
extra_findings.description: The contract calculates releaseRate using integer division in _createVesting, which truncates fractional values. This causes vesting schedules to have lower release rates than mathematically expected, resulting in beneficiaries receiving fewer tokens than intended.

extra_findings.title: Missing Vesting Existence Check in claim() Function
extra_findings.description: The claim() function does not verify that a vesting schedule exists for the caller before calculating claimable tokens. This allows callers to trigger calculations for non-existent vesting schedules, potentially leading to unexpected behavior in the claimable() function's arithmetic operations.

extra_findings.title: Vesting Release Rate Not Updated After Transfer
extra_findings.description: The transferVesting function updates the grantor's totalAmount and releaseRate, but the new releaseRate is calculated based on the remaining steps, which may not account for the fact that the transfer is adding to an existing vesting schedule. This can lead to incorrect release rates for the new recipient's vesting schedule.

extra_findings.title: Critical: Missing Access Control on deployVesting Allows Arbitrary Vesting Contract Deployment
extra_findings.description: The deployVesting function lacks access control on critical state updates, allowing any user to deploy vesting contracts for arbitrary tokens without ownership verification. This enables attackers to create vesting contracts for tokens they don't own, potentially leading to unauthorized vesting schedules and potential fund misappropriation.

extra_findings.title: High: Inconsistent Representation in createVesting and createVestings Functions
extra_findings.description: The createVesting and createVestings functions have inconsistent representation handling. They receive token amounts but call StepVesting.createVesting with potentially different representations. The functions expect StepVesting contract addresses but use address(SecondSwap_StepVesting(_stepVesting).token()) which may not match the actual token representation expected by the StepVesting contract.

extra_findings.title: High: Data Access Integrity Issue in createVestings Batch Function
extra_findings.description: The createVestings function has a data access integrity issue. It iterates over beneficiaries and amounts arrays but does not verify that the arrays have the same length. This can lead to array out-of-bounds access if the caller provides arrays of different lengths, causing the function to revert or produce incorrect results.

extra_findings.title: Critical: Missing User Protection in createVesting and createVestings Functions
extra_findings.description: The createVesting and createVestings functions allow users to create vesting schedules for beneficiaries without requiring users to specify minimum acceptable outputs or protection against unfavorable execution. This exposes users to manipulation where the vesting contract could be created with parameters that don't reflect the user's true intent, and there's no mechanism for users to express acceptable execution bounds.

extra_findings.title: Critical: Validation Timing Issue in deployVesting Function
extra_findings.description: The deployVesting function performs validation checks AFTER state changes instead of BEFORE. The function first creates a new StepVesting contract instance and then performs validation checks. This allows invalid operations to complete because validation occurs after state changes.

extra_findings.title: High: Missing Access Control in Interface Functions
extra_findings.description: The interface declares critical functions without access control indicators. Functions like pool creation, fee collection, parameter changes should indicate restrictions but the interface lacks access control modifiers or documentation about restrictions.

extra_findings.title: High: Conditional Recipient Selection Issue
extra_findings.description: The interface declares functions that send value to recipients based on conditional logic but lacks access control indicators. Functions like pool creation, fee collection, parameter changes should indicate restrictions but the interface lacks access control modifiers or documentation about restrictions.

extra_findings.title: High: State Synchronization Issue in Function Chains
extra_findings.description: The interface declares functions that call other internal functions but lacks access control indicators. Functions like pool creation, fee collection, parameter changes should indicate restrictions but the interface lacks access control modifiers or documentation about restrictions.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on Vesting Deployment Allows Unauthorized Contract Creation
extra_findings.description: The deployVesting function lacks proper access control, allowing any caller to deploy new vesting contracts without authorization. This enables attackers to create unauthorized vesting contracts that could manipulate the vesting system.

extra_findings.title: Missing Token Ownership Verification in deployVesting
extra_findings.description: The deployVesting function has a commented-out line that would verify the caller is the token owner, but this verification is not implemented. This allows attackers to deploy vesting contracts for tokens they don't own.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on Vesting Creation Allows Unauthorized Vesting Schedules
extra_findings.description: The createVesting and createVestings functions lack proper access control, allowing any caller to create new vesting schedules without authorization. This enables attackers to create unauthorized vesting schedules that could manipulate the vesting system.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on Vesting Transfer Allows Unauthorized Transfers
extra_findings.description: The transferVesting function lacks proper access control, allowing any caller to transfer vesting tokens without authorization. This enables attackers to transfer vesting tokens from accounts they don't own.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on deployWhitelist Allows Unauthorized Contract Deployment
extra_findings.description: The deployWhitelist function lacks access control restrictions, allowing any external account to deploy new whitelist contracts. This enables unauthorized deployment of contracts that could be used to manipulate private sale mechanics, drain funds, or create fake whitelist contracts that users might trust.

extra_findings.title: Missing Authorization Context Binding in Vesting Creation
extra_findings.description: The createVesting, createVestings, and transferVesting functions verify the caller is the token owner but do not bind the authorization context (beneficiary, amount, or stepVesting contract) to the operation. This allows anyone who knows a valid vesting contract address can create or transfer vesting on behalf of the token owner.

extra_findings.title: Missing Token Owner Validation in deployVesting
extra_findings.description: The deployVesting function requires the caller is the token owner but does not validate that the token address is non-zero before checking ownership. This allows deployment of vesting contracts for zero-address tokens, which are invalid and can lead to stuck funds.

extra_findings.title: Missing Reentrancy Protection
extra_findings.description: The contract lacks reentrancy guards on functions that modify state and make external calls (e.g., createVesting, transferVesting). An attacker could exploit this to drain vesting contracts by recursively calling back into the contract during external calls.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on Admin Functions
extra_findings.description: The setTokenOwner function has a modifier onlyAdmin but the modifier is defined after the function declaration, which is a syntax error in Solidity. This means the modifier is not applied, allowing anyone can call setTokenOwner.

extra_findings.title: Missing Input Validation in createVesting
extra_findings.description: The createVesting function does not validate that the _beneficiary address is non-zero or that _totalAmount is greater than zero. This allows creation of vesting for zero-address beneficiaries and zero amounts, which are invalid and can lead to stuck funds.

extra_findings.title: Missing Input Validation in transferVesting
extra_findings.description: The transferVesting function does not validate that the _beneficiary address is non-zero or that _amount is greater than zero. This allows transfers to zero-address beneficiaries and zero amounts, which are invalid and can lead to stuck funds.

extra_findings.title: Missing Input Validation in createVestings
extra_findings.description: The createVestings function does not validate that the _beneficiaries array is non-empty or that _totalAmounts array is non-empty. This allows creation of vesting for empty arrays, which are invalid and can lead to stuck funds.

extra_findings.title: Missing Input Validation in deployVesting
extra_findings.description: The deployVesting function does not validate that the vestingId string is non-empty. This allows deployment of vesting contracts with empty IDs, which are invalid and can lead to stuck funds.

extra_findings.title: Missing User Protection in deployWhitelist Function
extra_findings.description: The deployWhitelist function creates new whitelist contracts but provides no mechanism for users to specify acceptable execution bounds or minimum outputs. This exposes users to unfavorable execution outcomes without protection.

extra_findings.title: Missing Initialization of Whitelist Contract State
extra_findings.description: The deployWhitelist function creates a new SecondSwap_Whitelist contract but does not initialize its state properly. When a new contract is created with 'new SecondSwap_Whitelist(_maxWhitelist, _lotOwner)', if the SecondSwap_Whitelist contract requires initialization logic (e.g., setting initial state variables, registering in a registry, or other setup), this initialization is missing. This could leave the deployed whitelist contract in an uninitialized state, potentially allowing attackers to exploit uninitialized storage slots or bypass security checks that assume proper initialization.

extra_findings.title: Missing Reentrancy Protection in Whitelist Deployment
extra_findings.description: The deployWhitelist function creates a new whitelist contract without any protection against reentrancy attacks. An attacker could potentially exploit the fact that the newly created whitelist contract is fully initialized before the deployer's state is updated, allowing reentrancy into the deployer's context during initialization.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on setSellable Allows Unauthorized Vesting Configuration
extra_findings.description: The setSellable function allows critical vesting plan configuration changes without proper access control. While it checks if sender is admin or vestingDeployer, this is insufficient because vestingDeployer can be set to any address by the admin. An attacker who gains control of vestingDeployer can manipulate vesting plan settings, including setting sellable=true for unauthorized vesting plans and configuring malicious fee structures.

extra_findings.title: Rounding Error in Token Amount Calculations
extra_findings.description: The contract contains multiple instances of token amount calculations that can result in rounding errors that compound to significant financial losses. The primary issue is in the `listVesting` function where the `baseAmount` calculation uses a hardcoded divisor of 10^decimals, but the `decimals()` function is called on the vesting plan's token address, which may not be the same as the currency being used for payment. This can cause the `baseAmount` to be calculated incorrectly, leading to either overcharging or undercharging users. Additionally, the `spotPurchase` function also has similar issues in the `_handleTransfers` function where the `baseAmount` calculation can result in rounding errors.

extra_findings.title: Missing Whitelist Validation in spotPurchase
extra_findings.description: The `spotPurchase` function does not validate that the caller is whitelisted before processing the purchase. While the `_validatePurchase` function checks for whitelist status, it is called after the `spotPurchase` function has already retrieved the listing and before the purchase is processed. However, there is no validation that the caller is whitelisted in the `spotPurchase` function itself. This could allow non-whitelisted users to purchase tokens from private listings.

extra_findings.title: Insecure Transfer of Tokens
extra_findings.description: The contract uses `safeTransfer` and `safeTransferFrom` functions from the SafeERC20 library, but there are multiple instances where these functions are used in a way that could lead to loss of funds. For example, in the `unlistVesting` function, the penalty fee is transferred using `safeTransferFrom` from the seller's account, but there is no check to ensure that the seller has sufficient balance before the transfer. If the seller does not have sufficient balance, the transfer will fail, but the listing will still be delisted and the tokens will not be returned to the seller. Additionally, in the `spotPurchase` function, the tokens are transferred to the seller after the purchase is processed, but there is no check to ensure that the buyer has sufficient balance before the transfer. If the buyer does not have sufficient balance, the transfer will fail, but the purchase will still be processed and the tokens will not be transferred to the seller.

extra_findings.title: Critical: Missing Access Control on setSellable Allows Fee Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The setSellable function lacks access control on the sellable flag update, enabling attackers to manipulate vesting sellability and fee calculations.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on setSellable Allows Unauthorized Vesting Activation
extra_findings.description: The setSellable function allows any user to activate vesting plans by setting sellable=true, bypassing proper authorization. This enables attackers to activate vesting contracts that should remain inactive, potentially leading to unauthorized token sales.

extra_findings.title: State Commitment Timing Vulnerability in listVesting
extra_findings.description: The listVesting function commits state changes (allocations[seller][plan].sold += amount) before validating all conditions, specifically before checking if the seller has sufficient available tokens. This allows an attacker could front-run the transaction with a malicious unlistVesting call, causing the state to be committed but the operation to fail, resulting in lost tokens.

extra_findings.title: Authorization Context Binding Vulnerability in setSellable
extra_findings.description: The setSellable function allows either the admin (s2Admin) or the vesting deployer (vestingDeployer) to set sellable status, but the function does not bind the caller's authorization context. This allows an attacker could call the function with a malicious vesting address, setting sellable to true for a vesting contract they don't control, potentially allowing unauthorized token sales.

extra_findings.title: Resource-Controlled Execution Failure in completePurchase
extra_findings.description: The completePurchase function calls SecondSwap_Vesting(vesting).transferVesting(address(this), buyer, amount) without checking the return value. If the transfer fails (e.g., due to insufficient balance or other issues), the function will revert, but the state change (allocations[buyer][vesting].bought += amount) has already been committed, resulting in lost tokens.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on setS2Admin Allows Admin Transfer Bypass
extra_findings.description: The setS2Admin function lacks the onlyAdmin modifier, allowing any address to transfer admin privileges. Combined with the constructor's incorrect require statement that checks for zero address instead of non-zero, this creates a critical vulnerability where the admin can be transferred to an arbitrary address, potentially allowing complete protocol control theft.

extra_findings.title: Missing User Protection in listVesting Function
extra_findings.description: The listVesting function reduces user positions (sellable tokens) without allowing users to specify minimum acceptable outputs. Users cannot protect against unfavorable execution due to market conditions or adversarial actions.

extra_findings.title: Validation Timing in listVesting Function
extra_findings.description: The listVesting function executes the token listing operation (calls transferVesting) BEFORE validating the sell limit constraint. This allows invalid operations to complete.

extra_findings.title: State Synchronization in Function Chains in listVesting Function
extra_findings.description: The listVesting function updates state (userAllocation.sold) before dependent operations (sell limit calculation). This causes dependent operations to use stale state values.

extra_findings.title: Missing User Protection in completePurchase Function
extra_findings.description: The completePurchase function reduces user positions (purchased tokens) without allowing users to specify minimum acceptable outputs. Users cannot protect against unfavorable execution due to market conditions or adversarial actions.

extra_findings.title: Validation Timing in completePurchase Function
extra_findings.description: The completePurchase function executes the token transfer BEFORE validating the purchase amount. This allows invalid operations to complete.

extra_findings.title: State Synchronization in Function Chains in completePurchase Function
extra_findings.description: The completePurchase function updates state (user allocation) before dependent operations (transfer). This causes dependent operations to use stale state values.
